label: thm:Ulam
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:Ulam}
Every Lie group is countably representable.

\label{cor:LC}
Every locally compact second countable topological group is countably representable.\qed

label: lem:generic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:generic}
Let $U \subseteq \mathbf{R}^q$ be a domain and let $f$ be a real-analytic function on $U$ that is algebraic over $F(z_1, \ldots, z_q)$. If $f$ vanishes at a point whose coordinates are algebraically independent over $F$, then $f$ vanishes identically on $U$.

title: Definition
body_md: We say that $x\in \mathbf{R}$ is \textbf{good at $n\in \mathbf{N}$} if both tuples $a_{T_x,n}$ and $a_{T_x, n+1}$ belong to $W_x$.

label: lem:tail
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: lem:extension
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:extension}
For every $n$ there is an embedding $J_n:\mathbf{R}\hookrightarrow k\{\{s\}\}$
extending $j_n$ such that, for every $x\in\mathbf{R}$ good at $n$,
\[
 J_n(x)\in\mathscr{O}_{k\{\{s\}\}},\qquad
 \operatorname{res}(J_n(x))=f_{x,n}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we define $J_n(x)$ for any $x$ that is good at $n$. Since $j_n(X_\alpha)$ is $\ell_{\alpha,n} + s u_\alpha$, the only choice is as follows. Consider the multivariate Taylor series of $g_x$ at the point $\ell_{T_x,n}(t)$. Evaluate that series at the variables $s u_\alpha$, where $\alpha$ indexes the coordinates of $T_x$. This defines a formal series $J_n(x)$ in $s$ whose coefficients depend on $t$. We claim that these coefficients of the $s$-series lie in $k$. Indeed, implicit differentiation expresses each derivative occurring in the definition of Taylor series as a rational expression in the coordinates, the branch value, and the polynomial coefficients together with their derivatives. Thus every Taylor series coefficient for the variables $s u_\alpha$ is a ratio of functions that are real analytic on a neighborhood of $[0,1]$ and algebraic over $F(t)$. Such ratios define elements of the field of fractions of $C^\omega_{F(t)}([0,1])$, which lies in $k$. This shows that, when viewed as a series in $s$, the coefficients are indeed in $k$.

Thus $J_n(x)$ belongs to $k[[s]] \subseteq \mathscr{O}_{k\{\{s\}\}}$ and its residue is the constant term of the Taylor series, namely, $\operatorname{res}(J_n(x))=f_{x,n}$, which is in $C^\omega_{F(t)}([0,1])$ as already observed after the definition of $f_{x,n}$.

\smallskip
Next, we want this choice of $J_n(x)$ for good $x$ to extend to a morphism
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Jn}
F(T)[\,x\in\mathbf{R}:x\text{ good at }n\,]\longrightarrow k\{\{s\}\}.
\end{equation}
For this to be possible, we need to check that polynomial relations over $F(T)$ are preserved. 
The compatibility argument used below follows the method of Parusiński--Rond~\cite[Theorem~4]{Parusinski-Rond} that we repeat in adapted form for convenience. Consider thus a finite family $(x_1, \ldots, x_r)$
of good elements and a polynomial relation among them with coefficients in $F(T)$; clear the coefficient denominators. 

Denote by $A$ the (finite) collection of all indices $\alpha$ with $X_\alpha\in T_{x_i}$ for some $i=1, \ldots, r$ together with all indices occurring in the coefficients of the relation. We obtain a convex domain $U$ in $\mathbf{R}^A$ by intersecting the pull-back of all $W_{x_i}$. Write the cleared relation as
\[
 Q(X_A,x_1,\ldots,x_r)=0,
                                                      
\]
where $Q$ is a polynomial with coefficients in $F$. The function
\[
Q(z_A,g_{x_1}(z),\ldots,g_{x_r}(z))
\]
on $U$ is analytic,
algebraic over $F(z_A)$, and zero at the algebraically independent
tuple $X_A$. Therefore it is identically zero by Lemma~\ref{lem:generic}.
This forces the local branches to respect every relation between their
actual real values, on the entire common neighborhood containing the arc.

Taking Taylor series along the arc preserves this identity; therefore,
\[
Q\big(j_n(T_A), J_n(x_1),\ldots, J_n(x_r)\big)=0 \kern3mm \text{in} \kern3mm k[[s]].
\]
Thus the original relation, including its base-field coefficients, is preserved. This justifies that $j_n$ extends indeed to a $F(T)$-algebra homomorphism as in~\eqref{eq:Jn} above.

Finally, since $\mathbf{R}$ is algebraic over $F(T)$, the ring $F(T)[\,x\in\mathbf{R}:x\text{ good at }n\,]$ is a field, so that this extension~\eqref{eq:Jn} is injective. Using moreover that $k\{\{s\}\}$ is algebraically closed, this embedding extends to $\mathbf{R}$ as stated.

label: thm:new
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:new}
There exists a subgroup of countable index in $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ that can be lifted to $G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In view of Theorem~1.5 in~\cite{Conversano-Monod}, it suffices to show that every connected simple Lie group with finite center is countably representable. We shall show that this holds for our given connected semisimple Lie group $G$.

Since $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ is linear, we know from Thomas's theorem that it acts faithfully on some countable set $X$. Let now $\Gamma<\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ be a subgroup of countable index in $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ that can be lifted to a subgroup $\widetilde \Gamma< G$. It suffices to verify that the $G$-action on $G/\widetilde \Gamma \times X$ is faithful. The kernel of the action on $G/\widetilde \Gamma$ meets $Z_G$ trivially, whereas the kernel of the $G$-action on $X$ is exactly $Z_G$. This confirms that the action on the product is faithful.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: In fact, Theorem~\ref{thm:new} is strong enough that one does not need to appeal to Thomas's result as above. Instead, after reducing to the case where $G$ is simple as a Lie group, one could directly act on $G/\widetilde \Gamma$ and use the fact that $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ is simple as an abstract group, as proved by Goto, Corollary~3 in~\cite{Goto69}.

label: thm:coho
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:coho}
There exists a non-unital subring $I$ of $\mathbf{R}$ of countable index such that every continuous cohomology class of $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ for any discrete trivial coefficients in any positive degree vanishes when restricted to the subgroup of countable index $\Gamma<\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ corresponding to $I$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let first $\Gamma$ be any group (without topology) and let $f_\tau \colon\Gamma\to \operatorname{Ad}(G)$ be a family of group homomorphisms indexed by $\tau\in[0, 1]$ such that $f_\tau(\gamma) \in \operatorname{Ad}(G)$ depends continuously on $\tau$ for any given $\gamma\in \Gamma$. Let $Z$ be an abelian group, considered as a discrete trivial module for both $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ and $\Gamma$. One very concrete way to implement the pull-back through $f_\tau$ from the continuous cohomology of $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ to the ordinary cohomology of $\Gamma$ is to use Moore's Borel cohomology $H^*_\mathrm{M}(\operatorname{Ad}(G), Z)$, in which case a $Z$-valued Borel cocycle can be restricted to a cocycle on $f_\tau(\Gamma)$, compare e.g. pp.~27--28 in~\cite{Moore76}. In order to use the continuity of the family $f_\tau$, we recall that in the present setting $H^*_\mathrm{M}(\operatorname{Ad}(G), Z)$ is isomorphic to the sheaf cohomology $H^*_\mathrm{Sh}(B_{\operatorname{Ad}(G)}, Z)$ of Milnor's join $B_{\operatorname{Ad}(G)}$ with coefficient in the constant sheaf also denoted by $Z$. This is proved by Wigner in~\cite{Wigner_PhD, Wigner73} but can be read also in Theorem~E of~\cite{Austin-Moore}. In the discrete case, the corresponding fact for $B_\Gamma$ is completely classical. Under these isomorphisms, the pull-back will be induced by the maps $Bf_\tau\colon B_\Gamma \to B_{\operatorname{Ad}(G)}$ determined by $f_\tau$. Our assumption provides a homotopy between $Bf_0$ and $Bf_1$, compare Theorem~8.1 in~\cite{Dold63}, and this implies that the corresponding maps in cohomology are identical, see e.g. Theorem~IV.1.1 in~\cite{Iversen}.

\medskip
We now apply this to the following set-up for Theorem~\ref{thm:coho}. Let $F={\mathbf{Q}^\mathrm{rc}}$ be the real-closure of the rationals and consider the $F$-subalgebra $A\subseteq \mathbf{R}$ provided by Theorem~\ref{thm:path} together with the path $\varphi_\tau\colon A\to\mathbf{R}$ of unital ring homomorphisms. Define $I=\ker \varphi_0$, which is a non-unital subring of $\mathbf{R}$ that has countable index as a subgroup. 

In order to realize $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)$ and $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ as matrix groups, we need to choose a basis of the Lie algebra. We can take the basis in such a way that the structure constants are integers, see Proposition~14.3 in~\cite{Raghunathan}. (This is not crucial: otherwise we could enlarge $F$ to contains all structure constants). Writing $d=\dim(\mathfrak g)$, the group $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)$ is now an algebraic subgroup of $\mathbf{GL}_d(\mathbf{R})$. The group $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)$ preserves the Killing form, which is non-degenerate by Cartan's characterization of semi-simplicity~\cite[I.1.42]{Knapp02}; therefore, $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)$ lies in fact in the subgroup $\mathbf{SL}^\pm_d(\mathbf{R})$ of matrices with determinant $\pm 1$. Thus $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ is in $\mathbf{SL}_d(\mathbf{R})$, and it is in fact the connected component of the identity of $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)$, see e.g. Corollary~6.5 in~\cite[II]{Helgason01}.

\medskip
Formally, restricting coefficients to $I$ means the following. Denote by $\mathbf{SL}_d(\mathbf{R}, I)$ the collection of matrices $M$ satisfying that $M-\mathrm{Id}$ has all its coefficients in $I$. This is a subgroup because $I$ is a subring. The fact that $I$ has countable index in $\mathbf{R}$ as an additive subgroup implies that  $\mathbf{SL}_d(\mathbf{R}, I)$ has countable index in $\mathbf{SL}_d(\mathbf{R})$, e.g. by considering that root subgroups generate the latter (compare also Remark~1 in~\cite{Ershov-Churkin}). Therefore, the group $\Gamma = \operatorname{Ad}(G) \cap \mathbf{SL}_d(\mathbf{R}, I)$ has countable  index in $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$.

We now define the homomorphisms $f_\tau \colon\Gamma\to \operatorname{Ad}(G)$ by applying entry-wise $\varphi_\tau$ to the matrix coefficients of $\Gamma$; we need to justify that the resulting matrix still lies in $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$. The structure equations defining $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)$ within $\mathbf{GL}_d(\mathbf{R})$ belong to $F$, so that  $f_\tau$ ranges in $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)$. On the other hand, since $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ is the identity component of that group and since $f_1(\Gamma) = \Gamma \subseteq \operatorname{Ad}(G)$, continuity of each individual $\tau\mapsto f_\tau(\gamma)$ implies that all of $f_\tau(\Gamma)$ remains in $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$.

At this point, we are in the setting considered in the first paragraph of the proof. The original inclusion of $\Gamma$ in $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ is realized by $f_1$, and we conclude that the pull-back to $\Gamma$ of the cohomology of $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$ can equivalently be done through $f_0$. However, $f_0(\Gamma)$ is the trivial group; the statement follows.
